planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; Sylvetta is a refined, more compact selection of wild arugula bred specifically for salad-mix growers and tolerates heat better than standard arugula.

directions: Scatter seed thinly over cool, fertile soil and cover lightly, since Sylvetta germinates best when kept consistently moist. This named selection of wild arugula produces smaller, more deeply lobed leaves than the species and a denser, more compact rosette that regrows readily after cutting. Its flavor is intensely nutty and peppery, sharper than salad arugula, and it holds up in heat and resists bolting far longer than Eruca types, making it a mainstay of Italian-style mesclun mixes. In mild-winter regions it behaves as a short-lived perennial and can be harvested for several seasons from the same planting.

planting.note: Direct sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring through fall; Runway was bred for a slower bolt response, extending the harvest window in warm weather compared to older arugula strains.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly into cool, moisture-retentive soil for fast, even germination. Runway produces smooth, rounded, dark green leaves with a clean, moderately spicy flavor and was selected by seed breeders for a notably slower bolt response, letting growers hold plantings longer into warm weather before they turn bitter and go to seed. It performs well both as a quick baby-leaf crop for salad mixes and, with wider spacing, as a full-size bunching arugula. Succession sow every couple of weeks for continuous cutting through the cool season.

planting.note: Sow 4-6 weeks before first frost for a fall and winter harvest, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; Vit is a classic large-leaved mâche selection favored for its vigorous, uniform rosettes.

directions: Sow seed thinly at a shallow depth in cool soil, since mâche germinates poorly once temperatures climb into summer range. Vit is a widely grown European strain prized for producing larger, rounder, more upright rosettes than generic corn salad, giving a better yield of tender leaves per plant. The mild, faintly nutty flavor and buttery texture make it a classic addition to winter salads, often paired with beets or walnuts in French cuisine. Rosettes tolerate hard frost and light snow cover, so plantings can be harvested through much of the winter with minimal protection.

planting.note: Sow in late summer for a fall and winter crop, or very early spring for a quick harvest before heat sets in; this French heirloom is named for its distinctive shell-shaped leaves.

directions: Direct sow shallowly into cool, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist through germination, which is slow and improved by a period of cold stratification if sowing in late summer heat. Coquille de Louviers is a traditional French heirloom named for its cupped, shell-like leaves, which form dense, slightly domed rosettes distinct from flatter mâche types. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving hard freezes under light mulch or row cover to provide fresh greens deep into winter. Harvest whole rosettes at the base and use raw in salads for its mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor.

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring for a quicker early-season harvest; Rhodos matures faster than heirloom Batavian types and tolerates a wider sowing window.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to allow heads room to fill out. Rhodos is a modern Batavian-type escarole bred for a fast, uniform habit with semi-savoyed, dark green outer leaves surrounding a naturally pale, self-blanching heart, sparing gardeners the need to tie leaves for blanching. It resists bolting and tipburn better than many older escarole strains, making it reliable for both spring and fall plantings. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for a milder, less bitter flavor than curly frisee types.

common_name: Corne de Cerf Chicory (Stag Horn Chicory)

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer for fall and winter cutting; this historic French chicory is named for its deeply antler-like, jagged leaf lobes.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained garden soil in full sun and thin young plants to give room for the sprawling rosette to develop. Corne de Cerf is an old French cutting chicory documented in nineteenth-century seed catalogs, prized for its long, narrow leaves cut into sharp, irregular lobes reminiscent of deer antlers, giving the variety its name. The leaves are eaten young as a pleasantly bitter salad green or cooked briefly like other chicories to mellow the flavor. It is closely related to the Catalogna and asparagus chicory group and, like them, can be allowed to bolt in late winter for tender, blanched inner shoots.

planting.note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before transplanting out; in most regions transplant in late summer for a fall harvest. Neos is a uniform hybrid frisee bred for reliable self-blanching and faster maturity than heirloom curly endives.

directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun once seedlings have several true leaves. Neos is a hybrid frisee endive selected for a compact, upright habit and finely cut, curled leaves that shade the heart naturally, producing a pale, tender center with little need for tying. It matures faster and more uniformly than many open-pollinated curly endives, which makes it a favorite among market growers for consistent harvests. Use the mildly bitter, delicate leaves raw in composed salads such as salade lyonnaise, or briefly wilted with warm bacon dressing.
